props.title: Better Than Chocolate
props.initialSlug: Lesbian love blooms amid family chaos & chocolate

sections.content: Better Than Chocolate (1999) emerged during a pivotal moment for LGBTQ+ cinema in the late 1990s, alongside films like But I'm a Cheerleader (1999) and All Over Me (1997). This Canadian romantic comedy broke new ground by treating its lesbian romance with warmth and authenticity rather than tragedy or sensationalism. Director Anne Wheeler crafted an intimate portrait of young love between Maggie, a bookstore worker, and Kim, an artist, while weaving in complex family dynamics and transgender representation through the character of Judy.

sections.content: The film's bookstore setting, Ten Percent Books, reflects the vital role of LGBTQ+ spaces in the 1990s. Similar safe havens appear in Go Fish (1994) and High Art (1998), highlighting how these community spaces fostered connection before mainstream acceptance. Wheeler's decision to include multiple queer storylines - from young love to mature relationships to gender identity - created a richer tapestry than many contemporary LGBTQ+ films. SUBHEAD: Breaking the Tragic Queer Narrative

Better Than Chocolate deliberately subverts the "bury your gays" trope common in films like The Children's Hour (1961) and Basic Instinct (1992). Instead, it embraces joy, humor, and hope while still addressing serious issues like censorship and family acceptance. This approach influenced later films like Imagine Me & You (2005) and D.E.B.S. (2004), proving LGBTQ+ stories could be both meaningful and uplifting.
